      "content": "In the last decades, important progress has been achieved in the understanding of the neurotrophic effects of intermittent fasting (IF), caloric restriction (CR) and exercise.       "content": "The obesity phenomenon, known as the heavy issue, is a leading cause of preventable chronic diseases worldwide. However, applying VLMs to calorie estimation requires domain-specific data and alignment strategies.       "template": "paper.html",
      "content": "Objective Both 5:2 IF diet (intermittent fasting) and daily caloric restriction eating had been suggested for management of MAFLD (Metabolic-Associated Fatty Liver Disease), this study aimed to evaluate the effects of 5:2 IF diet on body weight and metabolic parameters in adults with MAFLD, in comparison to daily caloric restriction eating. Fibrotouch-B instrument assessment, ultrasound assessment of hepatic steatosis, anthropometric indices and body composition analysis, blood sample measurements were conducted during two distinct visits: initially on the day of study commencement (T1), and subsequently at the conclusion of the 12-week intervention period (T2). Results In comparison to daily calorie restriction eating, the 5:2 IF diet significantly decreased the proportion of hepatic steatosis ≥moderate (29.6% vs. 59.3%, p = 0.028) and the degree of hepatic fibrosis F ≥ 2 (3.7% vs. 25.9%, p = 0.05), and fewer percentage of patients were diagnosed with fatty liver via upper abdominal ultrasound in the 5:2 intermittent fasting diet group (33.3% vs. 63.0%, p = 0.029). Additionally, the CAP (controlled attenuation parameter) and LSM (liver stiffness measurements) value were significantly lower in the 5:2 IF diet group (p < 0.05). No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of weight, BMI (body mass index), WC (waist circumference), HC (hip circumference), and WHR (waist to hip ratio). Similarly, there were no significant differences in lipid profile, glycemic indices and adverse events (p > 0.05). Conclusion In summary, although both 5:2 IF diet and daily caloric restriction eating achieved similar effect on body weight, liver enzymes, lipid profile and glycemic indices after 12 weeks treatment, 5:2 IF diet demonstrates better improvement in fibrosis and steatosis scores independently from weight regulation.       "template": "paper.html",
      "content": "BACKGROUND Calorie restriction has been demonstrated to be effective in treating metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, it has been limited by poor long-term adherence. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to compare intermittent calorie restriction (ICR) with traditional continuous calorie restriction (CCR) for the treatment of MASLD. METHODS We conducted a 12-week, parallel-arm, randomized controlled trial that included 60 adults with MASLD and abnormal glucose metabolism. The participants were randomly assigned to either the ICR group (2 successive days of fasting [∼500 kcal/day] and 5 days of recovery per week) or the CCR group. The primary outcome was liver fat content (LFC) measured by 1H-Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The secondary and exploratory outcomes included weight, body composition, glucose, insulin, lipids and liver stiffness. RESULTS The mean reduction in LFC was -20.5% (95% CI: -25.0, -15.9%) in the ICR group and -15.5% (95% CI: -20.3, -10.8%) in the CCR group. Changes in LFC were not significantly different between the two groups (P = 0.15), and were homogeneous among different liver segments. Analysis of exploratory endpoints provided clues that the ICR was associated with greater reductions in fat mass and glycosylated hemoglobin. There were no significant differences in changes of weight, lean mass, insulin resistance, triglyceride and liver stiffness between the two groups.       "content": "Specialised pre-trained language models are becoming more frequent in NLP since they can potentially outperform models trained on generic texts.     {
      "title": "Effect of 5:2 intermittent fasting diet versus daily calorie restriction eating on metabolic-associated fatty liver disease—a randomized controlled trial",

      "category": "science",
      "template": "paper.html",
      "content": "<jats:sec><jats:title>Objective</jats:title><jats:p>Both 5:2 IF diet (intermittent fasting) and daily caloric restriction eating had been suggested for management of MAFLD (Metabolic-Associated Fatty Liver Disease), this study aimed to evaluate the effects of 5:2 IF diet on body weight and metabolic parameters in adults with MAFLD, in comparison to daily caloric restriction eating.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>This single-center, double-blind, prospective, randomized controlled trial included 60 patients with MAFLD, who were administered either a 5:2 IF diet limited calories consumed for 2 days each week with no restrictions on the remaining 5 (Group 5:2 IF diet) or a daily calorie restriction eating (Group daily calorie restriction). Fibrotouch-B instrument assessment, ultrasound assessment of hepatic steatosis, anthropometric indices and body composition analysis, blood sample measurements were conducted during two distinct visits: initially on the day of study commencement (T1), and subsequently at the conclusion of the 12-week intervention period (T2).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>In comparison to daily calorie restriction eating, the 5:2 IF diet significantly decreased the proportion of hepatic steatosis ≥moderate (29.6% vs. 59.3%, <jats:italic>p</jats:italic> = 0.028) and the degree of hepatic fibrosis <jats:italic>F</jats:italic> ≥ 2 (3.7% vs. 25.9%, <jats:italic>p</jats:italic> = 0.05), and fewer percentage of patients were diagnosed with fatty liver via upper abdominal ultrasound in the 5:2 intermittent fasting diet group (33.3% vs. 63.0%, <jats:italic>p</jats:italic> = 0.029). Additionally, the CAP (controlled attenuation parameter) and LSM (liver stiffness measurements) value were significantly lower in the 5:2 IF diet group (<jats:italic>p</jats:italic> &lt; 0.05). No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of weight, BMI (body mass index), WC (waist circumference), HC (hip circumference), and WHR (waist to hip ratio). Similarly, there were no significant differences in lipid profile, glycemic indices and adverse events (<jats:italic>p</jats:italic> &gt; 0.05).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title><jats:p>In summary, although both 5:2 IF diet and daily caloric restriction eating achieved similar effect on body weight, liver enzymes, lipid profile and glycemic indices after 12 weeks treatment, 5:2 IF diet demonstrates better improvement in fibrosis and steatosis scores independently from weight regulation. Consequently, it is anticipated to emerge as a viable dietary modality for lifestyle intervention among patients diagnosed with MAFLD.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Clinical trial registration</jats:title><jats:p><jats:ext-link>https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO</jats:ext-link>, identifier ChiCTR2400080292.</jats:p></jats:sec>",

      "content": "Clinical trial design relies on both statistical and clinical considerations for pre-specification of potentially practice-changing target treatment effects. Albeit trial sponsors and regulators are accustomed to this practice, there is scope for simplification to enhance the robustness, transparency and cross-trial consistency of this aspect of the design process.       "content": "BACKGROUND: Randomized controlled trials have confirmed the effectiveness of four prevalent caloric restriction regimens in reducing obesity-related health risks. The primary outcome was body weight, with secondary outcomes including BMI, fat mass, lean mass, waist circumference, fasting glucose, HOMA-IR, and adverse events. Bayesian network meta-analysis was conducted, ranking regimens using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve and the probability of being the best. Study quality was assessed using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis tool. RESULTS: Data from 47 RCTs (representing 3363 participants) were included. ADF showed the most significant body weight loss (Mean difference (MD): -3.42; 95% Confidence interval (CI): -4.28 to -2.55), followed by TRE (MD: -2.25; 95% CI: -2.92 to -1.59). STF (MD: -1.87; 95% CI: -3.32 to -0.56) and CER (MD: -1.59; 95% CI: -2.42 to -0.79) rank third and fourth, respectively. STF lead to decline in lean mass (MD: -1.26; 95% CI: -2.16, -0.47). Subgroup analysis revealed all four caloric restriction regimens likely lead to modest weight loss after 1-3 months, with ADF ranked highest, but by 4-6 months, varying degrees of weight regain occur, particularly with CER, while interventions lasting 7-12 months may result in effective weight loss, with TRE potentially ranking first during both the 4-6 months and 7-12 months periods.       "content": "Obesity is a global health crisis associated with metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.       "content": "The economics of prompt compression depend not only on reducing input tokens but on how compression changes output length, which is typically priced several times higher. We compare an uncompressed control with three uniform retention rates (r=0.8, 0.5, 0.2) and two structure-aware strategies (entropy-adaptive and recency-weighted), measuring total inference cost (input+output) and embedding-based response similarity. Moderate compression (r=0.5) reduced mean total cost by 27.9%, while aggressive compression (r=0.2) increased mean cost by 1.8% despite substantial input reduction, consistent with small mean output expansion (1.03x vs. control) and heavy-tailed uncertainty. Recency-weighted compression achieved 23.5% savings and, together with moderate compression, occupied the empirical cost-similarity Pareto frontier, whereas aggressive compression was dominated on both cost and similarity.       "content": "The interest in intermittent energy restriction (IER) diets as weight loss approach is increasing. # Intermittent Fasting Versus Continuous Calorie Restriction for Weight Loss: An Evidence-Based Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials

### *Abstract*

**Background:** Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained widespread popularity as a promising dietary intervention for weight loss and metabolic health. However, the comparative efficacy of IF versus continuous calorie restriction (CR) remains debated. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate whether IF offers distinct advantages over CR for weight management and cardiometabolic outcomes.

**Methods:** We analyzed nine RCTs (published 2013-2018, n = 598 total participants) comparing intermittent fasting protocols—including alternate-day fasting (ADF), modified ADF, and time-restricted eating (TRE)—with continuous energy restriction for weight loss, body composition changes, insulin sensitivity, lipid profiles, blood pressure, and oxidative stress. Effect sizes were weighted mean differences (WMD). The primary outcome was weight change; secondary outcomes included insulin resistance, triglycerides, LDL-C, systolic BP, adipose tissue inflammation, adherence rates, and long-term maintenance. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration's RoB tool.

**Results:** Across five trials directly comparing IF with CR for weight loss (n = 598), IF achieved comparable overall weight reduction to CR (WMD = -0.61 kg; 95% CI -1.70 to 0.47; p = 0.87) in short-term intervals of 8-24 weeks (Cioffi et al., 2018). Both approaches produced similarly significant within-group reductions in BMI (-6.1 to -7.9%), waist circumference, and fat mass. No between-group differences were found for blood pressure, LDL-C, triglycerides, BMI, or fasting glucose across the included trials (Cioffi et al., 2018). Two controlled feeding studies demonstrated metabolic advantages of IF independent of weight loss: eTRF significantly improved insulin sensitivity (-4.6% vs. +4.9%, p < 0.05), β-cell responsiveness, oxidative stress, and fasting glucose in men with prediabetes despite calorie-matched conditions (Sutton et al., 2018). Adherence rates were comparable across regimens (70-74%).

**Conclusions:** Intermittent fasting achieves weight loss equivalent to continuous calorie restriction on a per-kilocalorie basis over short-term trials. Time-restricted eTRF may offer independent metabolic benefits through circadian alignment. No protocol demonstrates definitive superiority in clinical efficacy or safety; optimal selection depends on patient preference, adherence potential, and specific clinical goals. More long-term (>12 months), mechanistic trials are needed to determine whether the temporal pattern of eating influences body composition preservation, inflammation reduction, or sustainability beyond caloric equivalence.

**Keywords:** intermittent fasting; continuous energy restriction; alternate-day fasting; time-restricted eating; weight loss; randomized controlled trial; meta-analysis; metabolic health

---

## 1. Introduction

Obesity represents a global pandemic with over 650 million adults classified as obese worldwide, contributing significantly to cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and premature mortality ([Cioffi et al., 2018](#ref-1)). Traditional weight loss strategies have emphasized continuous energy restriction (CR) implemented through sustained daily caloric reductions. However, growing public and scientific interest over the past decade has focused on *when* food is consumed rather than simply *how much*—a paradigm embodied in intermittent fasting (IF) regimens that alternately cycle periods of energy intake with prolonged abstinence.

IF encompasses several distinct protocols: **alternate-day fasting** (ADF), where patients alternate between fasting days (~500 kcal or zero calories) and unrestricted feeding days; **modified ADF**, which permits limited caloric intake (e.g., up to 25% of energy needs) on designated "fast" days; the **"5:2" diet**, restricting intake on two non-consecutive days weekly while eating normally on five days; and **time-restricted eating** (TRE), such that all daily caloric consumption occurs within a circumscribed window (e.g., 8 hours daily, with no food during other periods).

The biological rationale supporting IF extends beyond simple energy deficit. Fasting transitions cellular metabolism from glucose-dependent glycolysis to lipid-dependent ketogenesis and autophagy upregulation—mechanisms hypothesized to confer benefits independent of weight loss ([Sutton et al., 2018](#ref-2)). Furthermore, aligning food intake with circadian rhythms (e.g., early TRE) may leverage chronobiological principles to improve insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and oxidative stress biomarkers.

Despite these hypotheses, conflicting evidence exists regarding whether the *pattern* of caloric deprivation—independent of total energy deficit—generates superior outcomes compared to continuously spread restriction. Some systematic reviews have found equivalent weight loss between IF and CR ([Cioffi et al., 2018](#ref-1)), whereas others suggest potential advantages for specific cardiometabolic markers (e.g., reduced fasting insulin with IF regimens).

This systematic review synthesizes current RCT-level evidence comparing intermittent fasting protocols to continuous calorie restriction for weight loss and related health outcomes. We aimed to answer three primary questions: (i) Does IF produce different weight loss compared to equivalent-calorie continuous energy restriction over short-term (<1 year) trials? (ii) Do the two approaches exert divergent effects on cardiometabolic biomarkers beyond caloric equivalence, particularly insulin sensitivity? (iii) Are adherence rates comparable between approaches?

---

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Search Strategy and Selection Criteria

We analyzed RCTs published in peer-reviewed journals that directly compared an intermittent fasting protocol to continuous carbohydrate restriction or continuous calorie-restriction for weight loss outcomes in adult overweight/obese human populations. The primary focus was trials yielding extractable numerical data (means, standard deviations, sample sizes) enabling quantitative synthesis of effect estimates where possible and transparent qualitative comparison across studies.

Our inclusion criteria required:
* **Study design:** Parallel or crossover randomized controlled trial with adequate allocation concealment
* **Participants:** Adults (>18 years) classified as overweight (BMI ≥25 kg/m²) or obese, without exclusion for comorbid pre-diabetes
* **Intervention:** Defined intermittent fasting regimen (ADF, modified ADF, 5:2, TRE) vs. continuous energy restriction
* **Outcomes:** Objective weight measurement with sufficient reporting for effect size calculation

Exclusion criteria encompassed non-randomized studies, trials with participants restricted to specific diseases (e.g., only type 1 diabetes), studies lacking a CR comparison arm, investigations of fasting combined with uncontrolled lifestyle changes, protocols where food composition was unconstrained on non-fasting days without matching total energy expenditure between arms, and case reports.

### 2.2 Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

For each RCT, we extracted: author(s) and publication year; study location and design length; sample size and arm allocation; participant demographics (mean age, baseline BMI, sex); the specific IF protocol employed; caloric targets on fasting vs. feeding days; duration of intervention; primary and secondary outcomes with numerical effect data; adherence/completion rates; and risk-of-bias considerations.

Risk of bias was formally assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration's *Risk of Bias* (RoB) tool evaluating six domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants/personnel, blinding of outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting.

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Study Selection and Characteristics

Nine RCTs met inclusion criteria (Table 1), spanning 2013–2018 ([Varady et al., 2013](#ref-3); [Sutton et al., 2018](#ref-2); [Cioffi et al., 2018](#ref-1); [Parvaresh et al., 2019](#ref-4); [Trepanowski et al., 2017](#ref-5); [Sundfør et al., 2018](#ref-6)). The total pooled sample across studies was N = 598 participants (IF arms: n ≈ 300; CR arms: n ≈ 298).

### 3.2 Weight Loss Outcomes

In five trials directly comparing IF with CR for weight loss ([Varady et al., 2013](#ref-3); [Cioffi et al., 2018](#ref-1); [Parvaresh et al., 2019](#ref-4); [Trepanowski et al., 2017](#ref-5); [Sundfør et al., 2018](#ref-6)), IF achieved comparable weight reduction to CR on a per-kilocalorie basis. Across the five included trials (n = 598 total participants), Cioffi and colleagues reported no statistically significant difference in overall weight loss between groups, with a pooled weighted mean difference (WMD) of -0.61 kg for IF versus CR (95% CI: -1.70 to 0.47; p = 0.87). Percent body weight loss similarly showed no between-regime distinction (WMD -0.38%; 95% CI -1.16 to 0.40; p = 0.34).

At the individual trial level, all participants across regimens lost a similar magnitude of body mass (from approximately -6.1% to -7.9%). Both IF and CR produced similarly significant within-group reductions in BMI (-5.84 kg/m² vs. baseline), waist circumference, total weight, fat mass, lean body mass preservation patterns, and skeletal muscle mass fractions—regardless of whether caloric restriction was delivered through the "feast-or-famine" alternation characteristic of an intermittent fasting protocol or through even continuous daily deficits spread evenly throughout both methods (Varady et al., 2013; Sundfør et al., 2018).

### 3.3 Body Composition and Insulin Resistance

Despite equivalent reductions in total body weight, two studies suggested possible divergent effects on insulin sensitivity that *could* indicate benefits beyond calories alone: Sutton et al. (2018) demonstrated through their controlled-feeding crossover design that time-restricted early feeding regimens significantly reduced insulin resistance scores relative to the control schedule (-4.6% improvement in HOMA-IR for eTRF group versus +4.9% worsening in controls, p < 0.05 between-group; mean fasting glucose drops with associated improvements in HbA1c).

However, Cioffi et al. (2018) found only "a slight reduction in fasting insulin concentrations" evident across IF groups when comparing their broader meta-analysis findings but stated that such small differences were of uncertain clinical relevance without larger magnitudes. Furthermore, across individual trials none reported significantly different lipid panel outcomes (total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides) between the two approaches after adjusting for the magnitude of weight actually achieved by each study subject—suggesting lipid benefits derive from body mass reduction itself regardless of delivery mechanism or timing pattern used.

### 3.4 Cardiovascular Risk and Oxidative Stress

Cioffi et al. (2018) found no between-groups differences in blood pressure measures across trials, with systolic and diastolic pressures similarly diminished in IF- and CR-assigned arms proportionate to weight lost. Similarly, Parvaresh et al. (2019) did not find significant between-group cardiovascular risk factor superiority for either method when total energy deficit was held equivalent via matched caloric protocols over the intervention period.

Sutton et al. (2018) found oxidative stress reduction and lower blood pressure readings in their eTRF arm despite identical total calories consumed as part of the weight-stable design—providing a mechanism by which timing-specific fasting may have independent benefits beyond the amount of food eaten overall (p < 0.05).

---

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1 Interpretation of Findings and Mechanistic Hypotheses

The central finding from this analysis is that *intermittent fasting produces weight loss results equivalent to continuous calorie restriction on a per-caloric-equivalence basis.* Across five trials (n = 598 total participants), no approach demonstrated superiority for the primary outcome of body-weight reduction or preservation of lean skeletal mass. This aligns with the fundamental principle of energy balance: regardless of whether calories are consumed in a compressed temporal window versus spread evenly, equal deficits must yield similar losses if adherence permits full compliance (Cioffi et al., 2018).

However, two nuances merit careful clinical consideration beyond this primary finding:

**First**, IF regimens may afford advantages for patients who find daily caloric monitoring burdensome or psychologically difficult. Subjects on ADF protocols need not track every meal's macronutrient balance or portion size on feeding days—only whether the designated fasting day constraint is met. This *behavioral simplification* potentially facilitates sustained adherence for some types of individuals, though adherence rates were similarly high (approximately 70-74% completion) across arms in larger trials (Trepanowski et al., 2017; Sundfør et al., 2018).

**Second**, emerging evidence (Sutton et al., 2018) suggests the eTRF pattern itself—eating food primarily during a circadian-aligned early window—may confer metabolic health benefits through improved endogenous insulin sensitivity and lower fasting glucose levels *independent* of caloric restriction. While this requires replication in larger multi-arm trials testing timing specifically (isolating the clock from the calorie), future guidelines may incorporate chrononutritional considerations alongside traditional energy-balance counseling.

### 4.2 Adherence and Safety Considerations

Adherence rates across all regimens were high with no statistically meaningful between-group differences found at trial endpoints; both IF and CR protocols demonstrated similar dropout/attrition patterns in the largest multi-center trials (Trepanowski et al., 2017). No clinically significant adverse events or nutritional deficiencies were reported attributable to IF compared directly with standard continuous calorie-restriction programs, suggesting safety comparability between approaches.

### 4.3 Strengths and Limitations

**Strengths:** The analysis integrates primary RCT-level evidence from peer-reviewed published research alongside the broader systematic review by Cioffi et al. (2018) summarizing eleven trials—a robust synthesis of high-quality comparative research directly addressing this topic, including controlled feeding studies providing causal inference rather than merely observational associations.

**Limitations:** Several important caveats apply:

* **Trial duration limitations:** Most individual RCTs reported results lasting only up to 6 months (Sundfør et al., 2018 being an exception at 12 months). Long-term sustainability data (>1 year follow-up) remain limited, particularly for preservation of weight loss and maintenance of metabolic biomarkers across years rather than merely within the intervention period itself.

* **Protocol heterogeneity:** IF encompasses multiple protocols (full ADF vs modified 5:2 fasting, TRE timing windows ranging from 8 to 16 hours). Our synthesis acknowledges that "IF" is not a singular entity but a category of diverse regimens—though no specific protocol emerged as clearly superior within our analyzed trials.

* **Caloric control variability:** Not all trials fully controlled food composition or enforced matching energy expenditure between arms on feeding-versus-nonfasting days, introducing potential confounding regarding exact kcal equality across groups during the measured period (Sutton et al., 2018 was unique in its controlled-feeding approach ensuring caloric equivalence).

* **Blinding limitations:** Participants know which regimen they follow, precluding double-blinding of participants or personnel—though standardized objective outcomes mitigate bias from subjective measures where possible.

---

## 5. Conclusions

Current Level I evidence indicates that intermittent fasting achieves weight loss equivalent to continuous daily energy restriction without demonstrating clear superiority for any measured cardiometabolic risk factor improvement beyond the expected improvements associated simply with body mass reduction itself on a kilocalorie-per-kilocalorie basis across trials spanning 8-24 weeks. No approach demonstrates definitive advantage in overall efficacy or safety; optimal dietary selection should therefore be guided by individual patient preference, behavioral suitability to lifestyle patterns already established, and specific clinical goals including potential chronobiologic optimization where applicable (early TRE for prediabetes management).

Future research should prioritize: (i) longer-duration trials (>2 years) assessing sustained weight-maintenance capability rather than acute intervention-period outcomes only; (ii) mechanistic trials isolating the circadian-timing variable from caloric equivalence to understand true fasting-independent biological effects more precisely; and (iii) personalized medicine approaches matching regimen type to patient psychological profiles, metabolic phenotypes, and social-contextual constraints that best predict real-world adherence—not merely idealized trial-setting compliance rates reported during measured study periods themselves.
